docs.title: Conditional Beans
docs.text:
A portable CDI extension that enables a bean only when a condition matches the current deployment.

  • Target runtime: CDI 4.1 (jakarta.enterprise:jakarta.enterprise.cdi-api:4.1.0)
  • Verified on Weld 6.0.3.Final with Weld JUnit5
  • Core API: four types — @Conditional, @Conditionals, Condition, ConditionContext
  • Repeatable support: one container — @Conditionals, generated by the compiler
  • Two runtimes: CDI Full (portable extension) and CDI Lite (build compatible extension)
  • No runtime dependency beyond the CDI API

FluDa Conditional Beans is a working prototype for the Jakarta EE CDI issues jakartaee/cdi#869 and jakartaee/cdi#986.

Part of the FluDa toolkit — module source.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text: Artifact Package What it is fluda-conditional-beans-api io.github.fludakit.conditional Core API (@Conditional, @Conditionals, Condition, ConditionContext) and the built-in conditional annotations with their condition implementations. fluda-conditional-beans-full io.github.fludakit.conditional.full CDI Full runtime: portable extension that evaluates conditions at bootstrap and vetoes non-matching beans and producers. fluda-conditional-beans-lite io.github.fludakit.conditional.lite CDI Lite runtime: build compatible extension that evaluates conditions during build/enhancement with deferred validation.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
A bean whose condition does not match is not part of the deployment:

  • it is not injectable,
  • it does not show up in BeanManager.getBeans(...),
  • it produces no ProcessBean event.

An injection point that requires a vetoed bean fails the deployment with an unsatisfied-dependency error. A missing bean is therefore explicit, instead of silently degrading to a no-op at runtime.

The extension is registered through META-INF/services/jakarta.enterprise.inject.spi.Extension, so it is active in every deployment that has the artifact on the classpath.

docs.title: @Conditional
docs.text:
@Documented
@Retention(RUNTIME)
@Target({ TYPE, METHOD, FIELD, ANNOTATION_TYPE })
@Stereotype
@Repeatable(Conditionals.class)
public @interface Conditional {
    Class<? extends Condition<?>>[] value();
}

It may be placed on a bean class, a producer method or a producer field.

The annotation is repeatable, so several conditions can be declared on one element, one annotation each:

@ApplicationScoped
@Conditional(ChinaCondition.class)
@Conditional(DatabaseAvailable.class)
public class ChinaTaxCalculator implements TaxCalculator {
}

The array form carries the same meaning, and the two styles may be mixed — @Conditional({ A.class, B.class }) and two separate @Conditional annotations are collected together, and all of them have to match.

A condition declared on a stereotype is collected in addition to the ones declared on the bean, which is why a stereotype may add its own requirements without interfering with the bean.

The annotation is itself a CDI stereotype and may be used as a meta-annotation, which is how an application composes an annotation of its own.

docs.title: @Conditionals
docs.text: The container annotation required by the repeatable annotation mechanism of Java. The compiler generates it and fills it with the annotations that were written. It is not meant to be used directly — declaring several @Conditional annotations is enough — and it stays invisible in the deployment: a bean that declares several conditions reports the same stereotypes as one that declares a single condition.

docs.title: Condition
docs.text:
@FunctionalInterface
public interface Condition<A extends Annotation> {
    boolean matches(ConditionContext context, A annotation);
}

A condition is a plain class with a public no-argument constructor. It is instantiated by the container, not managed by CDI, and should be deterministic and side-effect free.

A condition is written against the annotation that declares it, so that it can read the values of that annotation without reflection:

public class ChinaCondition implements Condition<ConditionalOnCountry> {

    @Override
    public boolean matches(ConditionContext context, ConditionalOnCountry annotation) {
        return "CN".equals(context.getProperty(annotation.country()).orElse(null));
    }
}

The type argument decides which annotation the condition is handed:

The condition is written as It is handed The condition was declared by Condition<Conditional> the @Conditional annotation @Conditional(X.class) on the bean Condition<ConditionalOnProperty> the @ConditionalOnProperty annotation @ConditionalOnProperty(...) on the bean Condition<MyOwnAnnotation> the @MyOwnAnnotation annotation an annotation of the application that carries @Conditional

The choice is made by the type of the condition, so it is checked by the compiler and it stays consistent for every evaluation.

docs.title: ConditionContext
docs.text:
A read-only view of the deployment data available during evaluation. It exposes only what a bootstrap-time activation decision needs:

Method What it answers getProperty(String key) the value of a configuration property. A dotted key is also matched in a relaxed environment-variable form, so app.country and APP_COUNTRY both resolve. hasClass(String... className) whether all named classes are available to the deployment. hasBean(Class<?> beanClass, Class<? extends Annotation>... qualifiers) whether a bean of the given type and qualifiers is part of the deployment.

hasBean answers from the potential deployment model: the answer never depends on declaration order, and a bean that is later vetoed by a condition still counts as present for evaluation purposes.

docs.title: Built-in conditions
docs.text:
Annotation The bean is enabled when @ConditionalOnBean(T.class) every named bean type has a bean in the deployment. @ConditionalOnMissingBean(T.class) every named bean type has no bean in the deployment. @ConditionalOnClass(Foo.class) or @ConditionalOnClass(name = "...") every named class is on the classpath. @ConditionalOnMissingClass(name = "...") every named class is absent from the classpath. @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "...", havingValue = "...") the configuration entry is present, and has the expected value when havingValue is set. @ConditionalOnMissingProperty(name = "...") the named configuration entries are absent.

Classes are named, not referenced

@ConditionalOnClass accepts a fully qualified name as well as a class literal. In CDI an annotation cannot safely refer to a class that is absent: the annotation instance is created, but reading the attribute throws TypeNotPresentException. A name is resolved without loading the class, which is what makes the check possible at all.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text: Start with getting started to add the artifact, declare your first condition, and pick the runtime that fits your deployment.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide covers adding FluDa Conditional Beans to your project and declaring your first conditional bean.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• JDK 21 or later.
  • CDI 4.1 or later (jakarta.enterprise:jakarta.enterprise.cdi-api:4.1.0).
  • No runtime dependency beyond the CDI API.

docs.title: Adding the dependency
docs.text: Choose the runtime that matches your deployment.

docs.title: CDI Full
docs.text:
Use the portable extension when your application runs in a full CDI container — GlassFish, WildFly, Weld SE, or any other Jakarta EE runtime:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-conditional-beans-full</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

The full artifact depends on api transitively, so the core API types are on the classpath as well.

docs.title: CDI Lite
docs.text:
Use the build compatible extension when your application is built with a CDI Lite capable build-time extension processor — for example Quarkus Arc Lite:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-conditional-beans-lite</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

The lite artifact depends on api transitively as well.

docs.title: Declaring your first condition
docs.text:
A condition is a plain class with a public no-argument constructor. It is written against the annotation that declares it, so it can read that annotation's values without reflection.

Start with a condition that reads a configuration property:

public class ChinaCondition implements Condition<Conditional> {

    @Override
    public boolean matches(ConditionContext context, Conditional annotation) {
        return "CN".equals(context.getProperty("app.country").orElse(null));
    }
}

Then declare it on a bean:

@ApplicationScoped
@Conditional(ChinaCondition.class)
public class ChinaTaxCalculator implements TaxCalculator {
}

When app.country is not CN, the bean is not part of the deployment. It is not injectable, it does not show up in BeanManager.getBeans(...), and it produces no ProcessBean event.

The extension is registered through META-INF/services/jakarta.enterprise.inject.spi.Extension, so it is active in every deployment that has the artifact on the classpath — there is nothing else to enable.

docs.title: Composing your own annotation
docs.text:
Because @Conditional is a stereotype, it can be used as a meta-annotation. This is how the built-in conditions are written, and it is how an application declares an annotation of its own:

@Documented
@Retention(RUNTIME)
@Target({ TYPE, METHOD, FIELD })
@Conditional(ChinaCondition.class)
public @interface ConditionalOnCountry {
}

A condition written against that annotation is handed the annotation instance:

public class CountryCondition implements Condition<ConditionalOnCountry> {

    @Override
    public boolean matches(ConditionContext context, ConditionalOnCountry annotation) {
        return "CN".equals(context.getProperty("app.country").orElse(null));
    }
}

docs.title: Using the built-in conditions
docs.text:
The built-in conditions cover the cases that come up most often. They are plain annotations, so they compose with your own:

@ApplicationScoped
@ConditionalOnClass(name = "com.example.OptionalIntegration")
public class OptionalIntegrationBean {
}

@ApplicationScoped
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "app.country", havingValue = "CN")
public class ChinaTaxCalculator implements TaxCalculator {
}

@ApplicationScoped
@ConditionalOnMissingBean(LegacyPaymentService.class)
public class PaymentServiceConfiguration {
}

See the module overview for the full table of built-in conditions and the API they are built on.

docs.title: Combining conditions
docs.text:
All collected conditions have to match. The first one that does not match vetoes the bean. The repeatable form and the array form carry the same meaning and may be mixed:

@ApplicationScoped
@Conditional(ChinaCondition.class)
@Conditional(DatabaseAvailable.class)
public class ChinaTaxCalculator implements TaxCalculator {
}
